title: HealthBridge — AI-Powered Clinical Trial Patient Matching
content:
HealthBridge is transforming clinical trial recruitment through artificial intelligence. Our platform uses advanced natural language processing to match eligible patients from electronic health record (EHR) data to clinical trial criteria in real time, dramatically reducing the single largest bottleneck in drug development.

Clinical trials take an average of 18 months just to recruit enough patients. 80% of trials fail to meet enrollment timelines, costing the pharmaceutical industry billions of dollars annually and delaying life-saving treatments from reaching patients who need them.

HealthBridge changes this. Our AI engine analyzes complex, unstructured EHR data — physician notes, lab results, imaging reports, medication histories — and automatically identifies patients who meet specific trial eligibility criteria. We deliver 3x faster patient matching and 40% better retention rates compared to traditional recruitment methods.

Founded in 2023 by Dr. James Okafor, a former Pfizer clinical operations director, and Lisa Chen, formerly of Flatiron Health, HealthBridge combines deep clinical expertise with cutting-edge AI. We partner with leading academic medical centers and serve pharmaceutical companies ranging from mid-stage biotechs to top-20 global pharma.

Headquartered in Chicago, our team of 22 clinicians, data scientists, and engineers is on a mission to ensure no patient misses a trial that could save their life, and no trial fails because the right patients couldn't be found.

This costs pharma an estimated $8M per day in delayed revenue for a typical drug. The problem is getting worse as trials become more complex (precision medicine requires narrower patient criteria).

- **Solution**: HealthBridge uses NLP to parse unstructured EHR data and match patients against trial eligibility criteria. Their clinical language model is fine-tuned on millions of clinical notes. It handles the messiness of real medical records — abbreviations, inconsistent terminology, missing data.

Partnership with Northwestern Memorial Hospital as anchor clinical site. 3x faster matching vs traditional methods. 40% better patient retention (patients matched by HealthBridge are more likely to complete the trial because the matching is more precise).

- **Team**: Dr. Okafor brings the clinical domain expertise and pharma relationships. Lisa Chen (CTO) was at Flatiron Health for 4 years building their EHR analytics platform. Strong technical cofounder pairing.

- **Fundraise**: Raising Series A, targeting ~$14M. $4M seed from ARCH Venture Partners (2023). Current revenue $1.8M ARR.

This is a real problem with real customers paying real money. Dr. Okafor's Pfizer background gives him credibility with pharma buyers that most AI startup founders lack. The Northwestern partnership is a strong proof point. I want to go deeper.

title: HealthBridge — Technical Deep-Dive with Lisa Chen (CTO)
author: Maya Patel
content:
Meeting: Technical deep-dive — HealthBridge
Date: April 10, 2026
Attendees: Maya Patel (AIVC), Lisa Chen (CTO, HealthBridge)
Location: Zoom + screen share

## Summary

Spent 90 minutes with Lisa walking through the technical architecture, NLP pipeline, data privacy approach, and integration model. Came away impressed with the engineering quality and pragmatic design choices.

## Technical Architecture

- **NLP Pipeline**: Custom clinical language model fine-tuned on de-identified clinical notes from their Northwestern partnership. Built on a transformer architecture with domain-specific tokenization for medical terminology. Handles abbreviations, misspellings, negation detection (critical in clinical context — "no evidence of diabetes" vs "diabetes"), and temporal reasoning ("diagnosed 3 years ago").

- **EHR Integration**: Uses FHIR APIs as the primary integration method. This is the pragmatic choice — FHIR is the healthcare interoperability standard and most major EHR systems (Epic, Cerner) now support it. They are NOT building custom integrations per hospital, which would be a scaling nightmare. Lisa was clear about this design decision.

- **Matching Engine**: Multi-criteria matching with confidence scores. Handles inclusion/exclusion criteria, temporal constraints, lab value ranges. Returns ranked patient lists with explainability — clinicians can see WHY each patient was matched.

## Data Privacy

- **Federated Approach**: This is well-designed. Patient data never leaves the hospital's infrastructure. HealthBridge deploys a lightweight inference container inside the hospital's firewall. Only de-identified match results (patient IDs, confidence scores) are transmitted back. No PHI crosses the boundary.

- **Compliance**: HIPAA BAA with every hospital partner. SOC 2 Type II certified. They've been through security reviews with 3 pharma companies.

## Concerns

- **Scaling hospital integrations**: While FHIR is standard, every hospital deployment still requires IT coordination, security review, and infrastructure provisioning. Northwestern took 4 months. Lisa estimates future deployments at 6-8 weeks once they have a repeatable playbook, but this could be optimistic. Each hospital's EHR configuration is slightly different.

- **Model performance on non-Northwestern data**: The fine-tuning is heavily weighted toward Northwestern's clinical notes. Need to validate performance generalizes across other hospital systems.

## Technical Assessment

- **Innovation**: 7/10 — The clinical fine-tuning is genuinely hard to replicate (requires access to clinical data and domain expertise), but the underlying NLP techniques are well-established. A well-funded competitor with clinical data access could build something similar in 12-18 months.

- **Engineering Quality**: 8/10 — Clean architecture, good design decisions (FHIR-first, federated privacy), solid engineering team.

- **Defensibility**: 7/10 — The clinical fine-tuning and hospital partnerships create meaningful moats, but they're not insurmountable. The real defensibility will come from data network effects as they onboard more hospitals.

## Action Items

- [ ] Maya to write up technical assessment for David
- [ ] Request information on model performance metrics across different hospital systems
- [ ] Ask about roadmap for automated hospital deployment tooling

title: HealthBridge — Data Room Review and Commercial Deep-Dive
author: David Okonkwo
content:
Meeting: Data room review and commercial discussion — HealthBridge
Date: May 15, 2026
Attendees: David Okonkwo (AIVC), Dr. James Okafor (CEO), Lisa Chen (CTO)
Location: AIVC office, Chicago

## Summary

Third meeting. Walked through data room materials and went deep on financials, pipeline, and unit economics. My conviction is high after this session.

## Financial Review

- **Revenue**: $1.8M ARR as of April 2026. Growing 25% quarter-over-quarter (was $1.15M in Q4 2025). Revenue is contracted annual with quarterly billing.

- **Customers**: 8 active pharma clients. 2 top-20 pharma companies (one oncology-focused, one rare disease). 6 mid-stage biotechs. Zero churn to date — though the base is small and contracts are relatively young.

- **Pipeline**: 6 additional pharma companies in various stages. 2 are in paid pilot phase, 4 in active discussions. Dr. Okafor is confident in closing 3-4 by end of Q3.

- **Unit Economics**: Average contract value $150K/year. Implementation cost ~$30K (mostly hospital integration time). Payback period ~18 months. Gross margins 72% (will improve as hospital integrations become faster).

- **Burn**: ~$320K/month. Current runway: 10 months on existing cash.

## Commercial Discussion

- The wedge strategy is clear: start with patient matching for a specific therapeutic area at one hospital, prove ROI, then expand to more therapeutic areas and more hospital sites within the same pharma relationship. Top customer started with oncology trials at Northwestern and is now expanding to 3 additional sites.

- Dr. Okafor sees the clinical trials market as a $50B+ opportunity. Patient recruitment is estimated at $10-15B of that. HealthBridge's current TAM (pharma-sponsored trials, US market) is roughly $3-4B.

- Pricing model is per-trial-per-site. As pharma customers run more trials across more sites, revenue scales naturally.

## Fundraise Terms

- Seeking $14M Series A. ARCH Venture Partners will follow on with $3M. Looking for a lead to take $8-10M. Targeting ~$45M pre-money valuation.

- Use of funds: Expand engineering team (10 to 18), hire 3 commercial team members, expand hospital network from 1 to 8 sites, regulatory preparation for EU expansion.

## My Assessment

This is a conviction bet for me. The market is massive, the problem is visceral (patients literally die waiting for trials to recruit), and James Okafor is the right person to build this company. The 25% QoQ growth with zero churn is strong for a company at this stage. I want to bring this to IC with a recommendation to lead.

- [ ] Discuss allocation with Sarah — are we comfortable with $8M at $45M pre-money?
- [ ] Follow up with ARCH to understand their perspective and follow-on commitment
- [ ] Schedule IC discussion for late May

title: Market Research: Clinical Trials Recruitment Landscape
author: Elena Rodriguez
content:
From: Elena Rodriguez
To: David Okonkwo
Date: April 18, 2026
Subject: HealthBridge — Market Research Summary

David,

Here's my research on the clinical trials recruitment market. Let me know if you want me to go deeper on any section.

**Market Overview**:
- Global clinical trials market estimated at $80B annually and growing at 6% CAGR
- Patient recruitment and retention is consistently cited as the #1 challenge — accounts for roughly $10-15B of total spend
- Average trial recruitment period: 18 months. 80% of trials experience delays due to enrollment shortfalls
- The cost of delay is staggering — estimated $600K-$8M per day in lost revenue depending on the drug

**Competitive Landscape**:

1. **Medidata (Dassault Systemes)**: The 800-pound gorilla. Dominant in clinical trial data management (RAVE platform). Recently launched an AI module for trial design and site selection. Revenue ~$1B. Strength: existing relationships with every major pharma company. Weakness: AI is bolted on to legacy platform, not purpose-built. Patient matching is not their core focus.

2. **TrialSpark**: Raised $100M Series B (Jan 2026). Different model — they operate their own clinical trial sites and recruit patients directly. Vertically integrated approach. Not directly competitive with HealthBridge's hospital-embedded model, but fishing in the same pond of pharma budgets.

3. **Unlearn.ai**: Uses digital twin technology to reduce the number of control arm patients needed in trials. Interesting but different problem — they reduce sample size, HealthBridge accelerates recruitment of the full sample.

4. **Deep 6 AI**: Closest direct competitor. Also uses NLP on EHR data for patient matching. Raised $17M Series A in 2024. Based in LA. From what I can tell, their technology is less mature than HealthBridge's (no federated privacy approach, which limits hospital adoption).

5. **Legacy CROs** (IQVIA, Parexel, Covance): Traditional contract research organizations that handle recruitment through manual processes. Massive incumbents but technology-challenged.

**Key Takeaway**: The market is large and the pain is real. HealthBridge's closest competitor (Deep 6 AI) has raised more but appears technically behind. The real competitive risk is from incumbents like Medidata bolting on AI capabilities, but their approach is fundamentally different (top-down analytics vs bottom-up patient matching).

Happy to discuss.

Elena

title: AI-Powered Patient Matching Could Cut Clinical Trial Timelines by Years
author: Rebecca Torres
content:
AI-Powered Patient Matching Could Cut Clinical Trial Timelines by Years
By Rebecca Torres | STAT News | February 10, 2026

CHICAGO — In the race to bring new drugs to market, the biggest bottleneck isn't in the lab. It's in the waiting room.

Clinical trials in the United States take an average of 18 months just to recruit enough patients, a timeline that costs pharmaceutical companies billions and, more importantly, delays treatments from reaching patients who desperately need them. Now a Chicago-based startup called HealthBridge says it can cut that timeline dramatically using artificial intelligence.

HealthBridge, founded in 2023 by former Pfizer clinical operations director Dr. James Okafor and ex-Flatiron Health engineer Lisa Chen, has developed an AI platform that automatically matches patients in hospital electronic health record systems to clinical trial eligibility criteria. The company says its technology delivers patient matches three times faster than traditional methods and improves retention rates by 40 percent.

The company's approach centers on a partnership with Northwestern Memorial Hospital, where HealthBridge's AI engine analyzes de-identified patient records to identify trial candidates. The system processes complex medical histories, parsing physician notes, lab results, and medication records to determine eligibility.

"The fundamental problem is that clinical trial criteria are written in one language and medical records are written in another," Dr. Okafor told STAT. "A patient might be a perfect candidate for an oncology trial, but their eligibility is buried in thousands of pages of clinical notes that no coordinator has time to read."

The company currently works with eight pharmaceutical clients and has processed over 200,000 patient records through its platform. Early results are promising: in a recent oncology trial, HealthBridge identified eligible patients in an average of 48 hours compared to the typical 6-8 weeks for manual screening.

Privacy advocates have raised questions about AI systems accessing sensitive medical records, but HealthBridge says its federated architecture keeps patient data within hospital firewalls. The AI processes records locally and only transmits de-identified results.

The clinical trials recruitment market is attracting significant attention from investors and technology companies. Medidata Solutions, the Dassault Systemes subsidiary that dominates clinical trial data management, recently launched its own AI-powered module, while startups like TrialSpark and Deep 6 AI are also targeting different aspects of the recruitment challenge.

title: Medidata (Dassault Systemes) Launches AI Module for Clinical Trial Design
author: Mark Sullivan
content:
Medidata (Dassault Systemes) Launches AI Module for Clinical Trial Design
By Mark Sullivan | FierceBiotech | March 5, 2026

Medidata Solutions, the Dassault Systemes subsidiary that powers clinical trials for 20 of the top 25 global pharmaceutical companies, announced the launch of Medidata AI Studio, an artificial intelligence module integrated into its widely-used RAVE clinical trial platform.

The new module uses machine learning to optimize clinical trial design, including protocol optimization, site selection, and enrollment forecasting. Medidata says the tool can predict enrollment timelines with 85% accuracy and recommend protocol modifications to improve patient recruitment.

"AI is transforming every aspect of clinical development, and Medidata is uniquely positioned to lead this transformation," said Medidata CEO Rama Kondru. "With data from over 30,000 clinical trials and 9 million patients, we have the largest clinical trial dataset in the world to train our AI models."

The announcement signals Medidata's intent to compete with a growing crop of AI-native startups targeting the clinical trials space, including companies like HealthBridge, Deep 6 AI, and Unlearn.ai. While these startups have focused on specific pain points like patient matching and trial simulation, Medidata is positioning AI Studio as a comprehensive suite embedded within the platform that pharmaceutical companies already use.

Analysts noted that Medidata's approach — bolting AI capabilities onto an existing platform — differs fundamentally from startups building AI-native solutions from scratch. "The question is whether Medidata can move fast enough," said Endpoints News analyst Claire McCarthy. "They have the data advantage, but their platform is 20 years old. Rebuilding it around AI is not trivial."

Medidata AI Studio is available immediately to existing RAVE customers with pricing on a per-module basis.

title: TrialSpark Raises $100M Series B to Scale Virtual Clinical Trial Sites
author: Sarah Perez
content:
TrialSpark Raises $100M Series B to Scale Virtual Clinical Trial Sites
By Sarah Perez | TechCrunch | January 22, 2026

TrialSpark, the New York-based company that operates its own network of clinical trial sites to accelerate drug development, has raised $100 million in Series B funding led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from existing investors including Thrive Capital and Box Group.

The company, founded in 2017, takes a vertically integrated approach to clinical trials. Rather than relying on traditional academic medical centers and hospital networks, TrialSpark operates a growing network of purpose-built clinical trial sites staffed by its own physicians and coordinators. The company handles everything from patient recruitment to data collection, promising to cut trial timelines by 50% or more.

"We believe the future of clinical trials is purpose-built infrastructure, not retrofitting existing healthcare systems," said TrialSpark CEO Benjamin Robbins. "Our model gives us end-to-end control over the patient experience, which is why our retention rates are among the highest in the industry."

The fresh capital will fund the expansion of TrialSpark's site network from 15 to 50 locations across the United States, with plans to enter Europe by 2027. The company says it has run over 100 clinical trials to date for pharmaceutical clients ranging from early-stage biotechs to several top-20 pharma companies.

TrialSpark's approach sits in contrast to other clinical trials technology companies like Medidata (data management), HealthBridge (AI-powered patient matching within existing hospital systems), and Unlearn.ai (digital twin simulations). While these companies aim to improve the existing clinical trial infrastructure, TrialSpark is building a parallel system from scratch.

Critics have questioned whether TrialSpark's asset-heavy model can scale efficiently, noting the significant capital required to build and staff physical trial sites. But Robbins argues the unit economics improve dramatically with scale. "At 50 sites, our per-trial cost drops by 40%," he said.
